How well a model does on data it has never seen is called generalisation, and it is the
reason for fitting a model at all. A flexible enough model can fit its training stations perfectly
and still predict new sites worse than the average count. The four pages in this section
cover three ideas, on the same simulated survey as the rest of the course.

A perfect fit is a warning sign:

- **underfitting and overfitting**: a tree that fits every training station does worse
  on new sites than predicting the average, and making a tree more flexible step by step
  draws the U-shaped error curve.

The U-shaped curve comes from bias and variance:

- **the bias–variance trade-off**: as a tree gets more flexible, its bias falls and its
  variance rises; under both lies noise, the largest part of the error on the survey,
  and a random forest cuts the variance by averaging trees.

Complexity is chosen honestly:

- **regularisation**: every input added to a linear regression makes it more flexible,
  even a column of random numbers, and a penalty holds it back; ridge regression
  shrinks every coefficient, and the lasso sets some to zero;
- **hyperparameter selection**: a setting such as a tree's node size or the penalty's
  weight is chosen by cross-validation on the training sites, and the test sites are
  opened only once, at the end.

The section picks up threads from earlier ones.
[Decision trees](../03-supervised-learning/decision-trees.qmd) chose a tree's depth on
validation sites, and [Underfitting and overfitting](underfitting-and-overfitting.qmd)
names the two ways that choice can go wrong.
[Likelihood and priors](../04-how-algorithms-learn/likelihood-and-priors.qmd) showed that
a prior shrinks coefficients; [Regularisation](regularisation.qmd) tests whether that
helps on new sites.
[Splitting the data](../02-marine-data/splitting-data.qmd) set validation sites aside for
choosing a model; [Hyperparameter selection](hyperparameter-selection.qmd) replaces them
with cross-validation, which lets every training site take a turn.

## Further resources

**Documentation**

- [Tune model parameters](https://www.tidymodels.org/start/tuning/), tidymodels. `tune()`, a grid, and resampling used honestly.
- [Underfitting versus overfitting](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/model_selection/plot_underfitting_overfitting.html), scikit-learn. Three polynomial fits to the same points, which is this section's argument in one figure.
- [Tuning the hyper-parameters of an estimator](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/grid_search.html), scikit-learn user guide.
